hook: You deposit your paycheck, and the bank does not keep it in a drawer with your name on it. It keeps a small slice and lends the rest to someone buying a car. That borrower now has spendable money too, while your balance is untouched. This is how banks create money, and why a single deposit can support many times its size in new loans.

prereq.q: Which of these is counted in M1?
prereq.why: M1 counts currency held by the public and checkable deposits.

prereq.q: You deposit \$100 of cash into checking. What happens to M1 at that moment?
prereq.why: Currency turns into a checkable deposit; both are in M1.

figure.caption: A bank balance sheet: required reserves are deposits times the ratio, and excess reserves are what is left to lend.

chain.effect: it keeps the required reserves (deposits x ratio) and has excess reserves to lend

chain.cause: The bank lends its excess reserves
chain.effect: a new checkable deposit is created, so the money supply rises

chain.cause: The borrowed money is spent and redeposited in other banks
chain.effect: they lend again, so the money supply can grow by up to excess reserves x 1 / required reserve ratio

ideas: In fractional reserve banking, banks keep part of deposits as reserves and lend the rest. A balance sheet lists assets (reserves, loans, bonds) and liabilities (deposits).
Required reserves = deposits x required reserve ratio. Excess reserves = total reserves - required reserves. One bank can lend its excess reserves.

The money multiplier is 1 / required reserve ratio. The most the money supply can grow is excess reserves x the money multiplier. This is the limited reserves picture: banks hold few reserves beyond the required amount, so the reserve requirement limits lending.
A cash deposit does not change the money supply at first; new money is created when banks lend.

misconception.wrong: When \$1,000 of cash is deposited and the ratio is 0.1, the money supply grows by \$10,000.
misconception.right: The \$1,000 was already money. Only the \$900 of excess reserves is lent, so the money supply grows by at most \$900 x 10 = \$9,000.

summary: Banks hold a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend the rest. Required reserves are deposits times the required reserve ratio, which the central bank sets, and excess reserves are the rest of a bank's reserves. A bank creates money when it lends its excess reserves, because the loan becomes a new deposit. As loans are spent and redeposited, the money supply can grow by up to excess reserves times the money multiplier, 1 / required reserve ratio, less when banks hold extra reserves or people hold cash.
